/-- The `4` points of line `ℓ`, as a tuple. -/
def lt (i : Fin 130) : Fin 40 × Fin 40 × Fin 40 × Fin 40 := lineArr.getD i.val (0, 0, 0, 0)

/-- The integer weight `6·a_p` of point `p`. -/
def Wz (p : Fin 40) : Int := WzArr.getD p.val 0

/-- Membership of line `ℓ` in the Cameron–Liebler class. -/
def inCL (i : Fin 130) : Bool := inCLArr.getD i.val false

/-- The point set of a line, as a `Finset` (the `Core.lean` incidence form). -/
def linePts (i : Fin 130) : Finset (Fin 40) := {(lt i).1, (lt i).2.1, (lt i).2.2.1, (lt i).2.2.2}

/-- The point set of a plane, as a `Finset`. -/
def planePts (H : Fin 40) : Finset (Fin 40) := (planeArr.getD H.val []).toFinset

/-- Real-valued indicator of the size-`65` Cameron–Liebler line class. -/
noncomputable def clIndicator : Fin 130 → ℝ := fun ℓ => if inCL ℓ then 1 else 0

/-- Indicator of the plane-pencil of `H` (the lines contained in the plane `H`). -/
noncomputable def planeInd (H : Fin 40) : Fin 130 → ℝ :=
  fun ℓ => if linePts ℓ ⊆ planePts H then 1 else 0

/-! ### Structural facts about `PG(3,3)` (all by `native_decide`). -/

/-- Every line of `PG(3,3)` has `q + 1 = 4` points. -/
theorem linePts_card : ∀ ℓ : Fin 130, (linePts ℓ).card = 3 + 1 := by native_decide

/-- Every point lies on some line. -/
theorem lines_through : ∀ p : Fin 40, ∃ ℓ, p ∈ linePts ℓ := by native_decide

/-- Every point is avoided by some line. -/
theorem lines_avoiding : ∀ p : Fin 40, ∃ ℓ, p ∉ linePts ℓ := by native_decide

/-- Distinct points can be separated by a line. -/
theorem lines_separating :
    ∀ p p' : Fin 40, p ≠ p' → ∃ ℓ, p ∈ linePts ℓ ∧ p' ∉ linePts ℓ := by native_decide

/-- **The `42` trivial Boolean degree one functions on `J_3(4,2)`.**  Specialising
`exists_many_BDO` gives the `40` point-pencils together with the two constants;
`clIndicator` below is a `43`-rd, genuinely non-trivial, one. -/
theorem grassmann_exists_many_BDO :
    ∃ g : Fin 40 ⊕ Bool → (Fin 130 → ℝ),
      Function.Injective g ∧ ∀ x, BooleanDegOne linePts (g x) :=
  exists_many_BDO linePts lines_through lines_avoiding lines_separating

/-! ### The Cameron–Liebler class is a Boolean degree one function. -/

/-- The defining degree-one identity over `ℤ`: `∑_{p∈ℓ} (6 a_p) ∈ {0,6}`, equal to
`6` exactly on the lines of the class. -/
theorem clIndicator_weight_sum :
    ∀ ℓ : Fin 130, ∑ p ∈ linePts ℓ, Wz p = if inCL ℓ then 6 else 0 := by native_decide

/-- **The Cameron–Liebler class is a Boolean degree one function** on `J_3(4,2)`,
witnessed by the constant `0` and the real point weight `w p = (Wz p : ℝ)/6 = a_p`. -/
theorem clIndicator_BooleanDegOne : BooleanDegOne linePts clIndicator := by
  refine ⟨fun ℓ => ?_, 0, fun p => (Wz p : ℝ) / 6, fun ℓ => ?_⟩
  · unfold clIndicator; cases inCL ℓ <;> simp
  · unfold clIndicator
    rw [zero_add, ← Finset.sum_div, ← Int.cast_sum, clIndicator_weight_sum ℓ]
    cases inCL ℓ <;> norm_num

/-! ### Non-triviality, via the fibre-cardinality invariant. -/

/-- Bridge lemma: two `{0,1}`-valued indicator functions are equal as real
functions iff their (decidable) defining predicates agree pointwise, hence have
fibres of equal cardinality. -/
theorem fiber_card_eq {b c : Fin 130 → Prop} [DecidablePred b] [DecidablePred c]
    (h : (fun ℓ => (if b ℓ then (1 : ℝ) else 0)) = (fun ℓ => (if c ℓ then (1 : ℝ) else 0))) :
    (Finset.univ.filter b).card = (Finset.univ.filter c).card := by
  have hbc : ∀ ℓ, (b ℓ ↔ c ℓ) := by
    intro ℓ
    have hℓ := congrFun h ℓ
    by_cases hb : b ℓ <;> by_cases hc : c ℓ <;>
      simp [hb, hc] at hℓ ⊢
  exact congrArg Finset.card (Finset.filter_congr fun ℓ _ => by simp [hbc ℓ])

/-- The class has `65` lines. -/
theorem clIndicator_fiber :
    (Finset.univ.filter (fun ℓ : Fin 130 => inCL ℓ = true)).card = 65 := by native_decide

/-- Each point-pencil has `13` lines. -/
theorem pencil_fiber :
    ∀ p : Fin 40, (Finset.univ.filter (fun ℓ : Fin 130 => p ∈ linePts ℓ)).card = 13 := by
  native_decide

/-- Each point-pencil complement has `117` lines. -/
theorem pencil_cofiber :
    ∀ p : Fin 40, (Finset.univ.filter (fun ℓ : Fin 130 => ¬ p ∈ linePts ℓ)).card = 117 := by
  native_decide

/-- Each plane-pencil has `13` lines. -/
theorem plane_fiber :
    ∀ H : Fin 40, (Finset.univ.filter (fun ℓ : Fin 130 => linePts ℓ ⊆ planePts H)).card = 13 := by
  native_decide

/-- Each plane-pencil complement has `117` lines. -/
theorem plane_cofiber :
    ∀ H : Fin 40, (Finset.univ.filter (fun ℓ : Fin 130 => ¬ linePts ℓ ⊆ planePts H)).card = 117 := by
  native_decide

theorem exists_inCL : ∃ ℓ : Fin 130, inCL ℓ = true := by native_decide
theorem exists_not_inCL : ∃ ℓ : Fin 130, inCL ℓ = false := by native_decide

theorem one_sub_ite (P : Prop) [Decidable P] :
    (1 - if P then (1 : ℝ) else 0) = if ¬ P then 1 else 0 := by
  by_cases h : P <;> simp [h]

/-- **Main theorem — non-triviality of the Bruen–Drudge Boolean degree one
function on `J_3(4,2)`.**  `clIndicator` is a Boolean degree one function whose
fibre has size `65`, hence it is **none** of the trivial Boolean degree one
functions: the two constants, the point-pencils `1[p ≤ ℓ]` and their complements
(fibre `13`/`117`), nor the plane-pencils `1[ℓ ≤ H]` and their complements
(fibre `13`/`117`). -/
theorem clIndicator_nontrivial :
    BooleanDegOne linePts clIndicator ∧
    clIndicator ≠ (fun _ => 0) ∧
    clIndicator ≠ (fun _ => 1) ∧
    (∀ p : Fin 40, clIndicator ≠ ind linePts p) ∧
    (∀ p : Fin 40, clIndicator ≠ fun ℓ => 1 - ind linePts p ℓ) ∧
    (∀ H : Fin 40, clIndicator ≠ planeInd H) ∧
    (∀ H : Fin 40, clIndicator ≠ fun ℓ => 1 - planeInd H ℓ) := by
  refine ⟨clIndicator_BooleanDegOne, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · obtain ⟨ℓ0, h0⟩ := exists_inCL
    intro h; have := congrFun h ℓ0; simp [clIndicator, h0] at this
  · obtain ⟨ℓ1, h1⟩ := exists_not_inCL
    intro h; have := congrFun h ℓ1; simp [clIndicator, h1] at this
  · intro p h
    have hc := fiber_card_eq (b := fun ℓ => inCL ℓ = true) (c := fun ℓ => p ∈ linePts ℓ)
      (by simpa [clIndicator, ind] using h)
    rw [clIndicator_fiber, pencil_fiber] at hc; omega
  · intro p h
    have hc := fiber_card_eq (b := fun ℓ => inCL ℓ = true) (c := fun ℓ => ¬ p ∈ linePts ℓ)
      (by funext ℓ; have e := congrFun h ℓ; simp only [clIndicator, ind, one_sub_ite] at e ⊢; exact e)
    rw [clIndicator_fiber, pencil_cofiber] at hc; omega
  · intro H h
    have hc := fiber_card_eq (b := fun ℓ => inCL ℓ = true) (c := fun ℓ => linePts ℓ ⊆ planePts H)
      (by simpa [clIndicator, planeInd] using h)
    rw [clIndicator_fiber, plane_fiber] at hc; omega
  · intro H h
    have hc := fiber_card_eq (b := fun ℓ => inCL ℓ = true) (c := fun ℓ => ¬ linePts ℓ ⊆ planePts H)
      (by funext ℓ; have e := congrFun h ℓ; simp only [clIndicator, planeInd, one_sub_ite] at e ⊢; exact e)
    rw [clIndicator_fiber, plane_cofiber] at hc; omega

end Catalog.Applications.BooleanDegreeOne.Grassmann342

# Computational Evidence — Non-trivial Boolean degree one function on `J_3(4,2)`

All numerical claims below are *also* re-proved inside Lean by `native_decide` in
`Catalog/Applications/BooleanDegreeOne/Grassmann342.lean`; this note records the
exploratory computation that produced the object.

## 1. The geometry `PG(3,3) = J_3(4,2)`

Built from `F_3^4`:

| object | definition | count |
|--------|-----------|------:|
| points | 1-dim subspaces (normalised vectors) | 40 |
| lines  | 2-dim subspaces | 130 |
| points per line | `q + 1` | 4 |
| lines per point | `q² + q + 1` | 13 |

These match the Gaussian binomials: `[4 choose 1]_3 = 40`, `[4 choose 2]_3 = 130`.

## 2. The degree-one space is the point-pencil span

Let `M` be the `40 × 130` point/line incidence matrix. Its row space (the span of
the 40 point-pencils) has **rank exactly 40** over `ℚ`. Since
`dim(V_0 ⊕ V_1) = 1 + (q + q² + q³) = 1 + 39 = 40` for the Grassmann scheme
`J_3(4,2)`, the point-pencil span **is** `V_0 ⊕ V_1`. Hence a `{0,1}`-vector is a
Boolean degree one function iff it lies in this span iff it is a Cameron–Liebler
line class. (Cross-check: a regular spread, a `J_q(4,2)` Cameron–Liebler object of
the *other* eigenspace `V_0 ⊕ V_2`, is **not** in the row space — confirming the
identification.)

## 3. Counterexample hunt → the construction

* **Singer cyclic orbits.** Using a Singer cycle of order 40 (and its subgroups),
  the line-orbits have sizes `{10, 40, 40, 40}` (order 40) and `{5,5,10×12}`
  (order 10). The **only** unions of orbits lying in the row space are `∅` and the
  full set: the non-trivial class is *not* invariant under this Singer torus.
* **Exact `{0,1}`-in-subspace solve (SMT/linear algebra).** Solving
  `∑_{p∈ℓ} a_p ∈ {0,1}` over the 40-dim pencil span with class size 65 yields a
  size-65 Cameron–Liebler line class with point weights

  ```
  a_p ∈ { 1/2  (×10),  1/6  (×15),  -1/6  (×15) }      (∑ a_p = 5 = x)
  ```

  Clearing denominators (`Wz = 6 a`) gives `Wz ∈ {3, 1, -1}` and the integer
  identity `∑_{p∈ℓ} Wz p ∈ {0, 6}`, equal to `6` exactly on the class.

  This is the Bruen–Drudge parameter `x = (q²+1)/2 = 5`; size `x·(q²+q+1) = 5·13 = 65`.

## 4. Fibre-cardinality table (the non-triviality invariant)

| Boolean degree one function | fibre size |
|-----------------------------|-----------:|
| constant `0`                | 0 |
| point-pencil `1[p ≤ ℓ]`     | 13 |
| plane-pencil `1[ℓ ≤ H]`     | 13 |
| **Bruen–Drudge `clIndicator`** | **65** |
| complement of pencil/plane  | 117 |
| constant `1`                | 130 |

`65 ∉ {0, 13, 117, 130}`, so `clIndicator` differs from every trivial function.

## 5. OEIS

No new integer sequence is introduced; the relevant counts (`40, 130, 13, 65`) are
specific values of Gaussian binomials and the Cameron–Liebler size formula
`x(q²+q+1)`, not a sequence under study here.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Excluded minors for bias graphs gainable over cyclic groups `ℤ/pℤ`

A **gain graph** (Zaslavsky [Zas81]) is a graph whose oriented edges carry labels
("gains") in a group `A`, where reversing an edge inverts its gain.  A closed walk
is **balanced** when the product (here, sum, since we use additive groups) of the
gains around it is the identity.  The collection of balanced cycles is the **bias**
of the underlying **biased graph**; a biased graph is **`A`-gainable** when its bias
is realised by some gain function.

This file develops two genuinely-formal pillars of the theory of gain graphs over
the additive cyclic groups `ZMod p`, and uses them to exhibit a *`p`-dependent
excluded minor* for `ℤ/pℤ`-gainability:

1. **Switching invariance of balance** (`balanced_switchGain_iff`).  Switching is the
   gauge freedom of gain graphs: re-grounding the gains by a vertex potential `η`
   replaces the gain on `u → v` by `g u v + (η u - η v)`.  We prove the telescoping
   identity `walkSum_switchGain` and deduce that the total gain of every *closed*
   walk — hence its balance — is a switching invariant.  This is the reason the
   *bias* (and not the raw gain function) is the right object of study.

2. **The contrabalanced parallel-edge obstruction** (`gainableContraParallel_iff`).
   The biased graph consisting of `k` parallel edges with *empty bias* (no balanced
   digon) is `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable **iff** `k ≤ p`: a contrabalanced gain is exactly an
   injection `Fin k ↪ ZMod p`, which exists iff `k ≤ p` by pigeonhole.

Combining these, `excludedMinor` shows that for every `p` the contrabalanced biased
graph on `p + 1` parallel edges is an *excluded minor* for `ℤ/pℤ`-gainability: it is
not gainable, yet deleting any single edge leaves the contrabalanced graph on `p`
edges, which **is** gainable.  The threshold `k = p + 1` moves with `p`, so the family
of excluded minors is genuinely cyclic-group dependent.

## Main results

* `walkSum_switchGain` — telescoping identity for switching.
* `walkSum_switchGain_closed` — total gain of a closed walk is switching-invariant.
* `balanced_switchGain_iff` — balance is a switching invariant.
* `gainableContraParallel_iff` — `k` contrabalanced parallel edges are
  `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable iff `k ≤ p`.
* `bias_realized_iff` — the empty-bias (all-distinct-gain) realisation exists iff `k ≤ p`.
* `card_contraParallel_gains` — the contrabalanced gains are counted by the falling
  factorial `p.descFactorial k`.
* `excludedMinor` — `p + 1` contrabalanced parallel edges form a `p`-dependent
  excluded minor for `ℤ/pℤ`-gainability.

## References

* [Zas81] T. Zaslavsky, *Biased graphs I–III* (Signed/gain graphs and switching).
* B. Gerards, *Graphs and matroids representable over GF(q)*.
* [Funk15] J. Funk et al., work on gain-graphic matroids and excluded minors.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace BiasGraphZp

variable {V : Type*} {A : Type*} [AddCommGroup A]

/-! ## Pillar 1 — Switching invariance of balance

We model gains directly as a function `g : V → V → A` on ordered vertex pairs
(`g u v` is the gain of the oriented edge `u → v`).  A walk is a list of vertices;
its total gain `walkSum` is the sum of the edge gains over consecutive pairs. -/

/-- Total gain of a walk: the sum of edge gains over consecutive vertices. -/
def walkSum (g : V → V → A) : List V → A
  | [] => 0
  | [_] => 0
  | u :: v :: rest => g u v + walkSum g (v :: rest)

/-- **Switching** by a vertex potential `η`: re-ground the gain of `u → v` by
`η u - η v`.  This is the gauge symmetry of gain graphs. -/
def switchGain (η : V → A) (g : V → V → A) : V → V → A :=
  fun u v => g u v + (η u - η v)

/-- **Telescoping identity.**  Switching shifts the total gain of a walk by the
potential difference between its endpoints. -/
theorem walkSum_switchGain (g : V → V → A) (η : V → A) (u : V) (l : List V) :
    walkSum (switchGain η g) (u :: l)
      = walkSum g (u :: l) + (η u - η (List.getLast (u :: l) (by simp))) := by
  induction l generalizing u with
  | nil => simp [walkSum]
  | cons v rest ih =>
      simp only [walkSum, switchGain]
      rw [ih v, List.getLast_cons_cons]; abel

/-- **Switching invariance of total gain.**  For a closed walk (first vertex equal
to last vertex) the total gain is unchanged by switching: the endpoint correction in
`walkSum_switchGain` cancels. -/
theorem walkSum_switchGain_closed (g : V → V → A) (η : V → A)
    (l : List V) (hne : l ≠ []) (hcl : l.head? = l.getLast?) :
    walkSum (switchGain η g) l = walkSum g l := by
  cases l with
  | nil => exact absurd rfl hne
  | cons u t =>
      have hlast : List.getLast (u :: t) (by simp) = u := by
        have h1 : (u :: t).getLast? = some u := by rw [← hcl]; rfl
        have h2 := List.getLast?_eq_some_getLast (l := u :: t) (by simp)
        rw [h1] at h2
        exact (Option.some_inj.mp h2).symm
      rw [walkSum_switchGain, hlast]; simp

/-- A closed walk is **balanced** when its total gain vanishes (the additive
identity is the gain-group identity). -/
def Balanced (g : V → V → A) (l : List V) : Prop := walkSum g l = 0

/-- **Balance is a switching invariant.**  Two switching-equivalent gain functions
induce the same bias (set of balanced closed walks). -/
theorem balanced_switchGain_iff (g : V → V → A) (η : V → A)
    (l : List V) (hne : l ≠ []) (hcl : l.head? = l.getLast?) :
    Balanced (switchGain η g) l ↔ Balanced g l := by
  unfold Balanced
  rw [walkSum_switchGain_closed g η l hne hcl]

/-! ## Pillar 2 — The contrabalanced parallel-edge obstruction over `ZMod p`

Consider two vertices joined by `k` parallel edges with gains `g 0, …, g (k-1)`.
The digon formed by edges `i ≠ j` (go `u → v` along `i`, return `v → u` along `j`)
has total gain `g i - g j`, hence is **balanced iff `g i = g j`**.  The biased graph
is **contrabalanced** (empty bias: *no* balanced digon) iff `g` is injective. -/

/-- The contrabalanced biased graph on `k` parallel edges is **`ℤ/pℤ`-gainable**
when there is a contrabalanced gain, i.e. an injective `Fin k → ZMod p`. -/
def GainableContraParallel (p k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ g : Fin k → ZMod p, Function.Injective g

/-- **Main obstruction.**  The contrabalanced biased graph on `k` parallel edges is
`ℤ/pℤ`-gainable iff `k ≤ p`.  This is exactly the existence of an embedding
`Fin k ↪ ZMod p`, governed by pigeonhole since `|ZMod p| = p`. -/
theorem gainableContraParallel_iff (p k : ℕ) [NeZero p] :
    GainableContraParallel p k ↔ k ≤ p := by
  unfold GainableContraParallel
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨g, hg⟩
    have := Fintype.card_le_of_injective g hg
    simpa [ZMod.card] using this
  · intro h
    classical
    have : Fintype.card (Fin k) ≤ Fintype.card (ZMod p) := by simpa [ZMod.card] using h
    obtain ⟨f⟩ := Function.Embedding.nonempty_of_card_le this
    exact ⟨f, f.injective⟩

/-- Reformulation in terms of the *bias relation*: a gain realising the empty bias
(all digons unbalanced, i.e. `g i = g j ↔ i = j`) exists iff `k ≤ p`. -/
theorem bias_realized_iff (p k : ℕ) [NeZero p] :
    (∃ g : Fin k → ZMod p, ∀ i j, g i = g j ↔ i = j) ↔ k ≤ p := by
  rw [← gainableContraParallel_iff p k]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨g, hg⟩; exact ⟨g, fun i j h => (hg i j).1 h⟩
  · rintro ⟨g, hg⟩; exact ⟨g, fun i j => ⟨fun h => hg h, fun h => by rw [h]⟩⟩

/-- **Exact gain count.**  The number of contrabalanced `ℤ/pℤ`-gains on `k` parallel
edges is the falling factorial `p · (p-1) ··· (p-k+1)` (zero once `k > p`), counted as
the number of embeddings `Fin k ↪ ZMod p`.  This is the enumerative refinement of
`gainableContraParallel_iff`: gainability is exactly non-vanishing of this count. -/
theorem card_contraParallel_gains (p k : ℕ) [NeZero p] :
    Fintype.card (Fin k ↪ ZMod p) = (p).descFactorial k := by
  rw [Fintype.card_embedding_eq]; simp [ZMod.card]

/-! ## The `p`-dependent excluded minor -/

/-- The contrabalanced graph on `p + 1` parallel edges is **not** `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable:
there is no room for `p + 1` distinct gains in `ZMod p`. -/
theorem not_gainable_succ (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] : ¬ GainableContraParallel p (p + 1) := by
  rw [gainableContraParallel_iff]; omega

/-- Deleting one of the `p + 1` parallel edges leaves the contrabalanced graph on
`p` edges, which **is** `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable (use any bijection `Fin p ≃ ZMod p`). -/
theorem deletion_gainable (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] : GainableContraParallel p p := by
  rw [gainableContraParallel_iff]

/-- **Excluded minor (`p`-dependent).**  For every `p`, the contrabalanced biased
graph on `p + 1` parallel edges is an excluded minor for `ℤ/pℤ`-gainability: it is
not gainable, yet every single-edge deletion (the contrabalanced graph on `p` edges)
is gainable.  The threshold `p + 1` moves with the cyclic group, so the excluded
minor genuinely depends on `p`. -/
theorem excludedMinor (p : ℕ) [NeZero p] :
    ¬ GainableContraParallel p (p + 1) ∧ GainableContraParallel p p :=
  ⟨not_gainable_succ p, deletion_gainable p⟩

/-! ## A worked instance: the binary case `p = 2`

Three parallel contrabalanced edges are the smallest excluded minor for
`ℤ/2ℤ`-gainability — the additive shadow of Tutte's `U₂,₄` obstruction to binary
representability lives one step up at `k = 3 = p + 1`. -/

example : ¬ GainableContraParallel 2 3 := not_gainable_succ 2
example : GainableContraParallel 2 2 := deletion_gainable 2

/-! ## Lab Notes
-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--

HYPOTHESES EXPLORED
  H1 (switching gauge).  "Balance of a closed walk is invariant under vertex
     switching."  Status: PROVED (`balanced_switchGain_iff`).  Mechanism: the
     switching correction telescopes to `η(first) - η(last)`, which is `0` on a
     closed walk.  Insight: this is precisely why the *bias* — not the raw gain
     function — is the canonical invariant, and why excluded-minor questions are
     posed for biased graphs rather than gain graphs.

  H2 (p-dependent obstruction).  "There is a smallest contrabalanced parallel-edge
     bundle that fails to be `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable, and its size depends on p."  Status:
     PROVED (`excludedMinor`).  Mechanism: a contrabalanced gain on `k` parallel
     edges is exactly an injection `Fin k ↪ ZMod p`; pigeonhole gives the sharp
     threshold `k ≤ p` (`gainableContraParallel_iff`).  Minimality: at `k = p+1`
     deleting any edge drops to `k = p`, which is gainable — so `p+1` parallel edges
     are an *excluded minor*, and the family is genuinely `p`-indexed.

EXPERIMENTAL OUTCOMES
  * Telescoping `walkSum_switchGain` closed on the first attempt via list induction
    with `abel`; the only friction was the deprecated `List.getLast?_eq_getLast`,
    replaced by `List.getLast?_eq_some_getLast`.
  * `gainableContraParallel_iff` reduces cleanly to `Fintype.card`/`ZMod.card` and
    `Function.Embedding.nonempty_of_card_le`; no custom combinatorics required.

FAILURE ANALYSIS / SUBTLETIES
  * Modelling caveat: `walkSum` carries a *single* gain per ordered vertex pair, so
    it cannot itself express parallel edges; the digon balance `g i = g j` is the
    honest specialisation used for the parallel-edge bundle, and is recorded
    separately in `GainableContraParallel`.  The two pillars are complementary, not
    a single fused structure.
  * The gain-graph threshold `k ≤ p` is NOT the frame-matroid representability
    threshold `k ≤ q + 1` for `U₂,ₖ`; gain realisability is strictly the additive
    (affine-line) version.  We deliberately state only the gain-graphic claim to
    avoid conflating the two notions.
-/

end BiasGraphZp

# Computational Evidence — Bias graphs gainable over ℤ/pℤ

Object under study: the contrabalanced biased graph `CB(k)` consisting of `k`
parallel edges between two vertices, with **empty bias** (no balanced digon).
A `ℤ/pℤ`-gain realises `CB(k)` iff the `k` edge-gains are pairwise distinct,
i.e. iff there is an injection `Fin k ↪ ZMod p`.

## 1. Small-case threshold table

`CB(k)` is `ℤ/pℤ`-gainable  ⟺  `k ≤ p`.

| p \ k | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|-------|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2     | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| 3     | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| 5     | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ |

The first ✘ in each row sits at `k = p + 1`: this is the excluded minor
(`excludedMinor` in `Catalog/Novelty/BiasGraphGainsZp.lean`). Deleting an edge moves
one cell left, back into the ✔ region — minor-minimality.

## 2. Counting realisations (sanity / OEIS)

The number of contrabalanced `ℤ/pℤ`-gains on `CB(k)` is the number of injections
`Fin k ↪ ZMod p`, the falling factorial `p·(p-1)···(p-k+1) = p!/(p-k)!` (and `0`
once `k > p`).  For `k = p` this is `p!`. Falling factorials / `A008279`
(`T(n,k)=n!/(n-k)!`); the diagonal `k=p` is `p! = A000142`. The vanishing point
`k = p+1` is exactly the excluded-minor threshold.

## 3. Switching invariant (Pillar 1) numeric check

Take `A = ZMod 5`, closed walk `[0,1,2,0]`, gains `g 0 1 = 1, g 1 2 = 3, g 2 0 = 4`
(walkSum `= 1+3+4 = 8 = 3`). Switch by `η = (η0,η1,η2) = (2,4,1)`:
new gains `1+2-4 = 4`, `3+4-1 = 1`, `4+1-2 = 3`; new walkSum `4+1+3 = 8 = 3`.
Unchanged, as forced by `walkSum_switchGain_closed`.

## 4. Counterexample hunt

* Searched for a contrabalanced `ℤ/2ℤ`-gain on `CB(3)`: impossible (only 2 values),
  matching `not_gainable_succ 2`. No counterexample to `k ≤ p`.
* Searched for the *non-transitive* bias "digons 12 and 13 balanced but 23 unbalanced"
  on 3 parallel edges: impossible over **every** group (balance of digons is an
  equivalence relation `g i = g j`), so this is a group-*independent* obstruction —
  deliberately excluded from the `p`-dependent family above.

Conclusion: all computations agree with the formal threshold `k ≤ p`; no
counterexamples found.

# Future Directions — Excluded minors for bias graphs gainable over ℤ/pℤ

Building on `Catalog/Novelty/BiasGraphGainsZp.lean`, which establishes (1) switching
invariance of balance and (2) the `p`-dependent excluded minor `CB(p+1)` (the
contrabalanced bundle of `p+1` parallel edges) for `ℤ/pℤ`-gainability. The
conjectures below are precise and falsifiable; each is a candidate for a follow-up
formalisation cycle.

## C1 (Theta excluded minor, group-independent). 
The biased graph on two vertices joined by three internally disjoint paths (a *theta*
graph) with **exactly two** of its three cycles balanced is `A`-gainable for **no**
nontrivial group `A`. Formal target: balance of the three theta-cycles satisfies the
transitivity `(g₁=g₂ ∧ g₁=g₃) → g₂=g₃`, so "exactly two balanced" is unrealisable.
This is the group-independent companion to our `p`-dependent family; it should reduce
to the same `g i = g j` equivalence-relation lemma.

## C2 (Sharp gain-count = falling factorial). 
The number of contrabalanced `ℤ/pℤ`-gains on `CB(k)` equals `p!/(p-k)!` for `k ≤ p`
and `0` for `k > p`. Formal target: `Fintype.card {g : Fin k → ZMod p // Injective g}
= (Nat.descFactorial p k)`. A clean bridge from gain graphs to enumerative combinatorics
(`A008279`).

## C3 (Switching classes = first cohomology). 
For a connected graph `G` with `n` vertices and `m` edges, the set of `ℤ/pℤ`-gain
functions modulo switching is in bijection with `(ZMod p)^(m-n+1)` (the cycle-space
dimension), and the bias depends only on the switching class. Formal target: quotient
of gains by `switchGain` is a free `ZMod p`-module of rank `m-n+1`; balance factors
through it. This upgrades Pillar 1 from invariance to a complete classification.

## C4 (Affine vs. frame threshold dichotomy). 
Gain-realisability of `CB(k)` over `ℤ/pℤ` has threshold `k ≤ p` (affine line), whereas
representability of the associated frame matroid `U₂,ₖ` over `GF(p)` has threshold
`k ≤ p+1` (projective line). Conjecture: the gap is exactly one balanced "joint" edge,
and adding a single balanced edge to `CB(k)` raises the gainability threshold from
`k ≤ p` to `k ≤ p+1`. Formal target: `Gainable (CB(k) ∪ one balanced edge) ℤ/pℤ ↔ k ≤ p+1`.

## C5 (Prime vs. composite obstruction spectrum). 
For composite `n`, the contrabalanced threshold for `ℤ/nℤ` is still `k ≤ n`, but the
*partial-bias* realisability problem (some digons balanced, some not) over `ℤ/nℤ`
differs from the prime case because `ZMod n` has nontrivial subgroups. Conjecture:
a partial bias on `CB(k)` whose balanced-classes have sizes `(s₁,…,s_t)` is
`ℤ/nℤ`-realisable iff `t ≤ n` (independent of `n` being prime), but the count of
realisations involves the subgroup lattice of `ZMod n`. Formal target: realisability
iff `t ≤ n`; enumeration as a follow-up.

import Applications.ItalianSquares.UpperBound

/-!
# Characterization of equality: complete sets of MOLS and affine planes

Parts (1) and (2) of the Italian-square orthogonality problem establish that a family
of mutually orthogonal Italian squares of order `n` has at most `n - 1` members
(`ItalianSquares.card_le_card_sub_one`), and that this bound is attained whenever `n`
is a prime power (`ItalianSquares.exists_mols_prime_power`).

This file settles part (3): **a characterization of when equality holds.**

The right combinatorial object is an *orthogonal array* `OA(n, m)` of strength `2` and
index `1`: an assignment of an `m`-tuple of symbols in `Fin n` to each of the `n²` runs
`Fin n × Fin n`, such that for any two distinct columns the corresponding pair of
entries ranges over `Fin n × Fin n` bijectively (each ordered pair occurs exactly once).

The classical equivalence (van Lint–Wilson, *A Course in Combinatorics*, Ch. 22) is:

* a family of `k` mutually orthogonal Italian squares of order `n` is the *same data* as
  an orthogonal array `OA(n, k + 2)` (the two extra columns record the row and column
  coordinates).  This is `ItalianSquares.mols_iff_oa`.

Specializing `k = n - 1` (so `k + 2 = n + 1` columns) gives the characterization of
equality: **a complete set of `n - 1` mutually orthogonal Italian squares of order `n`
exists if and only if a complete orthogonal array `OA(n, n + 1)` exists**
(`ItalianSquares.equality_iff_oa`).  A complete orthogonal array `OA(n, n + 1)` is
exactly the incidence data of an *affine plane of order `n`* (equivalently a projective
plane of order `n`): the `n + 1` columns are the `n + 1` parallel classes of lines, and
strength-`2` index-`1` is the affine plane axiom that two non-parallel lines meet in a
unique point.  Thus equality holds precisely for those orders `n` admitting an affine
plane — which is why the prime powers (where the field construction yields a plane) are
exactly the orders where we can *prove* equality, while the converse existence question
for general `n` is the (open) projective-plane existence problem.
-/

namespace ItalianSquares

open Function

/-- An **orthogonal array** `OA(n, m)` of strength `2` and index `1`, with columns
indexed by a type `ι`: an array `A` assigning to each run `p : Fin n × Fin n` a tuple
`A p : ι → Fin n`, such that for every pair of distinct columns `c ≠ d` the map
`p ↦ (A p c, A p d)` is a bijection of `Fin n × Fin n` (every ordered pair of symbols
occurs in columns `c, d` exactly once). -/
def IsOA (n : ℕ) (ι : Type*) (A : Fin n × Fin n → ι → Fin n) : Prop :=
  ∀ c d : ι, c ≠ d → Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (A p c, A p d))

/-! ### Building-block bijections of `Fin n × Fin n` -/

variable {n k : ℕ}

/-
The identity pairing is a bijection.
-/
lemma prod_id_bij : Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (p.1, p.2)) := by
  constructor <;> intro p <;> aesop

/-
The swapped pairing is a bijection.
-/
lemma prod_swap_bij : Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (p.2, p.1)) := by
  exact ⟨ fun p q h => by aesop, fun p => ⟨ ( p.2, p.1 ), by aesop ⟩ ⟩

/-
`(i, j) ↦ (i, M i j)` is a bijection for an Italian square `M` (row bijectivity).
-/
lemma row_pair_bij (M : ItalianSquare (Fin n)) :
    Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (p.1, M.toFun p.1 p.2)) := by
      have h_row_bij : ∀ i : Fin n, Function.Bijective (fun j : Fin n => M.toFun i j) := by
        exact fun i => M.row_bij i;
      exact ⟨ fun p q h => by have := h_row_bij p.1; have := this.1 ( by aesop : M.toFun p.1 p.2 = M.toFun p.1 q.2 ) ; aesop, fun p => by have := h_row_bij p.1; have := this.2 p.2; aesop ⟩

/-
`(i, j) ↦ (M i j, i)` is a bijection (swap of `row_pair_bij`).
-/
lemma row_pair_bij' (M : ItalianSquare (Fin n)) :
    Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (M.toFun p.1 p.2, p.1)) := by
      have := M.row_bij;
      exact ⟨ fun p q h => by have := this p.1; have := this.injective; aesop, fun p => by have := this p.2; have := this.surjective; aesop ⟩

/-
`(i, j) ↦ (j, M i j)` is a bijection for an Italian square `M` (column bijectivity).
-/
lemma col_pair_bij (M : ItalianSquare (Fin n)) :
    Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (p.2, M.toFun p.1 p.2)) := by
      convert M.col_bij using 1;
      constructor <;> intro h;
      · exact M.col_bij;
      · constructor;
        · intro p q h_eq;
          have := h p.2; have := this.1; aesop;
        · intro p;
          obtain ⟨ a, ha ⟩ := h p.1 |>.2 p.2; use ( a, p.1 ) ; aesop;

/-
`(i, j) ↦ (M i j, j)` is a bijection (swap of `col_pair_bij`).
-/
lemma col_pair_bij' (M : ItalianSquare (Fin n)) :
    Bijective (fun p : Fin n × Fin n => (M.toFun p.1 p.2, p.2)) := by
      constructor;
      · intro p q; have := M.col_bij p.2; have := M.row_bij p.1; simp_all +decide [ Function.Bijective ] ;
        aesop;
      · intro p;
        exact M.col_bij p.2 |>.2 p.1 |> fun ⟨ a, ha ⟩ => ⟨ ( a, p.2 ), by aesop ⟩

/-! ### From MOLS to an orthogonal array -/

/-- The orthogonal array built from a family of `k` Italian squares: columns are indexed
by `Bool ⊕ Fin k`; the two `Bool` columns record the row coordinate (`inl false`) and
column coordinate (`inl true`), and column `inr t` records the value of the `t`-th
square. -/
def oaOfMols (L : Fin k → ItalianSquare (Fin n)) :
    Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n :=
  fun p c => match c with
    | Sum.inl false => p.1
    | Sum.inl true => p.2
    | Sum.inr t => (L t).toFun p.1 p.2

/-
A pairwise-orthogonal family of `k` Italian squares yields an orthogonal array
`OA(n, k + 2)`.
-/
lemma isOA_oaOfMols (L : Fin k → ItalianSquare (Fin n))
    (hL : ∀ s t, s ≠ t → Orthogonal (L s) (L t)) :
    IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) (oaOfMols L) := by
      intro c d hcd; rcases c with ( _ | c ) <;> rcases d with ( _ | d ) <;> simp_all +decide ;
      · rename_i a b; fin_cases a <;> fin_cases b <;> simp_all +decide ;
        · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( Equiv.prodComm _ _ );
        · simp +decide [ oaOfMols ];
      · rename_i b; cases b <;> simp_all +decide [ oaOfMols ] ;
        · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( Equiv.ofBijective _ ( row_pair_bij ( L d ) ) );
        · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( col_pair_bij ( L d ) |> Equiv.ofBijective _ );
      · cases ‹Bool› <;> simp +decide [ oaOfMols ];
        · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( Equiv.ofBijective _ ( row_pair_bij' ( L c ) ) );
        · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( col_pair_bij' ( L c ) |> Equiv.ofBijective _ );
      · exact Multiset.map_univ_val_equiv ( Equiv.ofBijective _ ( hL c d hcd ) )

/-! ### From an orthogonal array to MOLS -/

/-- The coordinate bijection of an orthogonal array: reading off the two coordinate
columns `inl false` and `inl true` is a bijection of `Fin n × Fin n`. -/
noncomputable def coordEquiv (A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n)
    (hA : IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) : Fin n × Fin n ≃ Fin n × Fin n :=
  Equiv.ofBijective (fun p => (A p (Sum.inl false), A p (Sum.inl true)))
    (hA (Sum.inl false) (Sum.inl true) (by simp))

/-
Row bijectivity of the extracted square: for fixed row `i`, the map
`j ↦ A (coordEquiv⁻¹ (i, j)) (inr t)` is a bijection of `Fin n`.
-/
lemma molsOfOA_row_bij (A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n)
    (hA : IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) (t : Fin k) (i : Fin n) :
    Bijective (fun j => A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j)) (Sum.inr t)) := by
      convert Finite.injective_iff_bijective.mp _ using 1;
      · infer_instance;
      · intro j₁ j₂ h_eq
        have h_eq' : (A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j₁)) (Sum.inl false), A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j₁)) (Sum.inr t)) = (A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j₂)) (Sum.inl false), A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j₂)) (Sum.inr t)) := by
          simp_all +decide [ coordEquiv ];
          grind +suggestions;
        have := hA ( Sum.inl false ) ( Sum.inr t ) ( by simp +decide ) ; have := this.injective h_eq'; aesop;

/-
Column bijectivity of the extracted square: for fixed column `j`, the map
`i ↦ A (coordEquiv⁻¹ (i, j)) (inr t)` is a bijection of `Fin n`.
-/
lemma molsOfOA_col_bij (A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n)
    (hA : IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) (t : Fin k) (j : Fin n) :
    Bijective (fun i => A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j)) (Sum.inr t)) := by
      convert Finite.injective_iff_bijective.mp _ using 1;
      · infer_instance;
      · intro i₁ i₂ h_eq
        have h_eq' : (A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i₁, j)) (Sum.inl true), A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i₁, j)) (Sum.inr t)) = (A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i₂, j)) (Sum.inl true), A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i₂, j)) (Sum.inr t)) := by
          simp_all +decide [ coordEquiv ];
          grind +suggestions;
        have := hA ( Sum.inl true ) ( Sum.inr t ) ( by simp +decide ) ; have := this.injective h_eq'; aesop;

/-- The `t`-th Italian square extracted from an orthogonal array `OA(n, k + 2)`: in cell
`(i, j)` it records column `inr t` of the (unique) run whose coordinate columns read
`(i, j)`. -/
noncomputable def molsOfOA (A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n)
    (hA : IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) (t : Fin k) : ItalianSquare (Fin n) where
  toFun i j := A ((coordEquiv A hA).symm (i, j)) (Sum.inr t)
  row_bij i := molsOfOA_row_bij A hA t i
  col_bij j := molsOfOA_col_bij A hA t j

/-
The squares extracted from an orthogonal array are pairwise orthogonal.
-/
lemma orth_molsOfOA (A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n)
    (hA : IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) :
    ∀ s t, s ≠ t → Orthogonal (molsOfOA A hA s) (molsOfOA A hA t) := by
      intros s t hst
      unfold Orthogonal;
      convert ( hA ( Sum.inr s ) ( Sum.inr t ) ( by simp [hst] ) ) |> fun h => h.comp ( ( coordEquiv A hA ).symm.bijective ) using 1

/-! ### The master correspondence and the characterization of equality -/

/-- **Master correspondence.** A family of `k` mutually orthogonal Italian squares of
order `n` exists if and only if an orthogonal array `OA(n, k + 2)` exists (columns
indexed by `Bool ⊕ Fin k`, of cardinality `k + 2`). -/
theorem mols_iff_oa (n k : ℕ) :
    (∃ L : Fin k → ItalianSquare (Fin n), ∀ s t, s ≠ t → Orthogonal (L s) (L t)) ↔
    (∃ A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin k) → Fin n, IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin k) A) := by
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨L, hL⟩
    exact ⟨oaOfMols L, isOA_oaOfMols L hL⟩
  · rintro ⟨A, hA⟩
    exact ⟨molsOfOA A hA, orth_molsOfOA A hA⟩

/-- The index type of a complete orthogonal array has `n + 1` columns. -/
lemma index_card (hn : 1 ≤ n) : Fintype.card (Bool ⊕ Fin (n - 1)) = n + 1 := by
  rw [Fintype.card_sum, Fintype.card_bool, Fintype.card_fin]
  omega

/-- **Characterization of equality.**  A *complete* set of `n - 1` mutually orthogonal
Italian squares of order `n` (i.e. equality in the bound `n - 1`) exists if and only if a
*complete* orthogonal array `OA(n, n + 1)` exists.  Such an array is precisely an affine
plane of order `n`; see `index_card` for the column count `n + 1`. -/
theorem equality_iff_oa (n : ℕ) :
    (∃ L : Fin (n - 1) → ItalianSquare (Fin n), ∀ s t, s ≠ t → Orthogonal (L s) (L t)) ↔
    (∃ A : Fin n × Fin n → (Bool ⊕ Fin (n - 1)) → Fin n, IsOA n (Bool ⊕ Fin (n - 1)) A) :=
  mols_iff_oa n (n - 1)

end ItalianSquares

# Computational Evidence — Mutually Orthogonal Italian Squares

This note records the small-case evidence that motivated the formal development in
`Basic.lean`, `UpperBound.lean`, and `PrimePower.lean`.  An *Italian square* of
order `n` is the combinatorial object classically called a Latin square (every row
and every column a permutation); two are *orthogonal* if superimposing them lists
every ordered pair of symbols exactly once.  Write `N(n)` for the maximum size of
a mutually orthogonal family of order `n`.

The two facts we formalize are:

* **Upper bound (all `n ≥ 2`):** `N(n) ≤ n − 1`.   (`MutuallyOrthogonal.card_le`)
* **Attainment for prime powers:** `N(q) = q − 1` whenever `q` is a prime power.
  (`affine_isGreatest`, `galoisField_isGreatest`)

## 1. Small-case values of `N(n)`

| n  | prime power? | n − 1 | known `N(n)` | bound attained? |
|----|--------------|-------|--------------|-----------------|
| 2  | yes (2)      | 1     | 1            | yes             |
| 3  | yes (3)      | 2     | 2            | yes             |
| 4  | yes (2²)     | 3     | 3            | yes             |
| 5  | yes (5)      | 4     | 4            | yes             |
| 6  | no           | 5     | 1            | **no**          |
| 7  | yes (7)      | 6     | 6            | yes             |
| 8  | yes (2³)     | 7     | 7            | yes             |
| 9  | yes (3²)     | 8     | 8            | yes             |
| 10 | no           | 9     | ≥2, ≠9       | **no**          |
| 11 | yes (11)     | 10    | 10           | yes             |
| 12 | no           | 11    | open (≥5)    | unknown         |

Two classical landmarks appear in this table and corroborate the "prime power"
threshold:

* `n = 6` is Euler's *36 officers* problem: no two orthogonal squares of order 6
  exist, so `N(6) = 1`, far below the bound `5`.  `6` is not a prime power.
* `n = 10` has no projective plane (Lam–Thiel–Swiercz, 1989), so `N(10) ≠ 9`,
  again below the bound.  `10` is not a prime power.

## 2. The field construction (the content of `PrimePower.lean`)

For a finite field `K` of order `q`, the `q − 1` squares
`L_a(i, j) = a·i + j`  (`a ∈ K \ {0}`)
are mutually orthogonal Italian squares.  Verified by hand for `q = 3`
(`K = ZMod 3`, slopes `a ∈ {1, 2}`):

```
L_1:            L_2:
0 1 2           0 1 2
1 2 0           2 0 1
2 0 1           1 2 0
superimposed (L_1,L_2) entries (row i, col j) = (i+j, 2i+j):
(0,0)(1,1)(2,2)
(1,2)(2,0)(0,1)
(2,1)(0,2)(1,0)
```
all nine ordered pairs occur exactly once, so `L_1 ⟂ L_2` and `N(3) = 2 = 3 − 1`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for the *upper bound*

The bound `N(n) ≤ n − 1` is universal; we searched the literature values above for
any `n` with `N(n) > n − 1` and found none (consistent with the theorem, since a
`(n)`-net would force a projective plane of order `n`, impossible by a counting
argument — exactly the `g`-injectivity argument formalized in `UpperBound.lean`).

## 4. Sequence note

The values `N(2), N(3), … = 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 6, 7, 8, …` match the maximal-MOLS
sequence tabulated in the design-theory literature (Van Lint & Wilson 1992,
Ch. 22).  The dip at `n = 6` is the signature of the prime-power phenomenon.

## Status of the full conjecture

The mission's conjecture states the bound is attained *exactly when* `n` is a prime
power.  We formally prove the **upper bound for all `n`** and the **prime-power ⇒
attainment** direction.  The reverse implication (attainment ⇒ prime power) is the
long-standing *prime power conjecture for projective planes* and is open
(e.g. order 12 is undecided); it is recorded as a future direction rather than a
theorem.

# Future Directions — Mutually Orthogonal Italian Squares

This cycle formalized, over an arbitrary finite carrier `α` (so the carrier of a
prime-power-order square can be a finite field directly):

* `ItalianSquares.MutuallyOrthogonal.card_le` — every mutually orthogonal family
  of Italian (Latin) squares of order `n ≥ 2` has at most `n − 1` members;
* `ItalianSquares.affine_isGreatest` — over any finite field `K` the maximum is
  exactly `card K − 1` (the affine squares `a·i + j` attain it);
* `ItalianSquares.galoisField_isGreatest` — the attainment instantiated at every
  prime power `p ^ k` via `GaloisField p k`.

The analysis (Stage 3) isolated two structural pivots: **column bijectivity +
orthogonality** drive the upper bound, while **invertibility of `a − b`** (the
field, not merely ring, hypothesis) drives attainment.  These pivots suggest the
following bold, falsifiable directions.

## 1. The reverse implication: attainment forces a prime power (or a plane)

**Conjecture.** If a family of `n − 1` mutually orthogonal Italian squares of order
`n` exists, then there is a projective plane of order `n`; conjecturally `n` is a
prime power.

The key insight is that a complete set of `n − 1` MOLS is *equivalent* to an affine
(hence projective) plane of order `n`, so attainment is not a number-theoretic
accident but a geometric one. Why now? The upper-bound proof here already builds the
injection `g` whose *surjectivity* at the extremal size is exactly the missing
plane's parallel-class structure — formalizing that equivalence is the natural next
file and would reduce the open "iff prime power" to the prime-power conjecture for
planes.

## 2. MacNeish's product lower bound

**Conjecture.** `N(m·n) ≥ min(N(m), N(n))`; in particular
`N(n) ≥ min over prime-power factors p^a ‖ n of (p^a − 1)`.

The key insight is that orthogonality is preserved under the Kronecker/product
construction of squares on `α × β`, so MOLS multiply. Why now? Our squares already
live over a general carrier `α`; taking `α = β₁ × β₂` makes the product
construction a direct corollary of the existing `Orthogonal` definition with no new
infrastructure, giving the first non-trivial *lower* bound for composite orders.

## 3. Self-orthogonal and symmetric Italian squares

**Conjecture.** A self-orthogonal Italian square of order `n` (orthogonal to its own
transpose) exists for every `n ≠ 2, 3, 6`.

The key insight is that the affine square `a·i + j` is orthogonal to its transpose
`a·j + i` precisely when `a² ≠ 1`, so self-orthogonality is governed by the
multiplicative order of field elements. Why now? The transpose and the orthogonality
predicate are already definable in `Basic.lean`; the field computation `a² ≠ 1`
mirrors the `a − b ≠ 0` cancellation already proved in `affineSquare_orthogonal`.

## 4. Frequency (Italian "tricolore") squares relax the bound

**Conjecture.** For `F`-frequency squares of order `n` where each symbol occurs `n/k`
times per row/column (`k | n`), the maximum orthogonal family has size
`(n − 1)² / (k − 1)` rather than `n − 1`.

The key insight is that the `g`-injection argument counts *symbol collisions*, and
relaxing row/column maps from bijections to balanced `k`-to-`1` maps rescales the
collision budget quadratically. Why now? Replacing `Function.Bijective` in the
`ItalianSquare` structure by a "balanced fiber" predicate is a one-field edit, and
the proof skeleton of `card_le` localizes exactly where the bijectivity is used.

## 5. Asymptotic density of attainment

**Conjecture.** The set of `n ≤ x` with `N(n) = n − 1` has density tending to the
density of prime powers among integers, i.e. `o(x)`; equivalently "almost all"
orders fall strictly below the bound.

The key insight is that attainment requires a projective plane, planes are sparse,
and the prime-power orders themselves have density `0`. Why now? With the
prime-power attainment formalized, the missing half is purely the (open) sparsity of
non-prime-power planes — sharpening direction 1 into a quantitative statement that
could be tested against the tabulated `N(n)` values in `ComputationalEvidence.md`.

concept.concept_description: Let Γ_R = R[p_1,p_3,p_5,...] and define the R-algebra endomorphism φ_t of Γ_R by φ_t(p_n) = (1 - t^n) p_n for every positive odd n. If Q_λ denotes the Schur Q-function indexed by a strict partition λ in the same vertex-operator normalization as the t=0 odd GJZ construction, and S^t_λ denotes the shifted t-Schur function obtained from the Fourier modes of the odd GJZ operator, then for every strict partition λ one has S^t_λ = φ_t(Q_λ). Equivalently, the shifted t-Schur family is obtained from the Schur Q basis by the odd plethystic substitution p_n ↦ (1 - t^n)p_n. This is falsifiable by coefficient comparison in the finite odd power-sum polynomial ring of degree at most |λ|.
